article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ)
description: The MSLQ is Pintrich's widely used self-report instrument for measuring SRL and motivation. The review reports it "is composed of 15 scales, divided into a motivation section with 31 items, and a learning strategies (SRL) section with 50 items" subdivided into cognitive, metacognitive and resource management scales. Its strength is combining SRL and motivation measures, offering detailed information about students' learning strategy use. Versions exist for college and high school students, and two recent reviews found it the most used instrument in SRL and in self-efficacy measurement.
requirements: Used as a self-report instrument combining motivation and learning strategies scales
target_learning_goals: measuring motivation and learning strategy use
examples: The review cites reviews by Roth et al. and Honicke and Broadbent finding the MSLQ the most used instrument in SRL and self-efficacy measurement
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: Effects of a Structured Decoding Curriculum on Adult Literacy Learners’ Reading Development
citation: Alamprese, J. A., MacArthur, C. A., Price, C., & Knight, D. (2011). Effects of a Structured Decoding Curriculum on Adult Literacy Learners' Reading Development. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555294
title: Making Sense of Decoding and Spelling (MSDS): a structured adult decoding curriculum based on Venezky's morphophonological analysis of English orthography
description: MSDS is a study-developed curriculum designed to teach adult learners to decode and spell words more accurately and fluently, beginning with basic alphabetic decoding and teaching the most common and useful patterns of English words. Its "core theoretical framework for the curriculum is Venezky's work (1970; 1999) on orthography", requiring analysis of morphemes and phonemes and their relationships, consistent with stage theories of spelling development. It embeds explicit metalinguistic information, a metacognitive strategy for decoding multisyllabic words, untimed repeated reading of 50-75 word passages, integrated spelling practice, whole-group scripted lessons, and progress-monitoring assessments about every five lessons.
requirements: Delivered as one component of a comprehensive adult reading course combined with vocabulary and comprehension instruction
Instructor training via two 2-day workshops plus technical assistance
constraints: Designed for efficiency given limited instructional time typical in ABE classes; no curriculum can teach all morphophonemic patterns used in skilled reading
target_learners: Adult basic education learners at the Low-Intermediate level (roughly fourth-to-seventh-grade reading comprehension)
target_learning_goals: Accurate and fluent decoding and spelling of English words
examples: Lessons open with informative texts containing the taught patterns and close with paired repeated reading of a brief smooth-reading passage
key_sources: Alamprese, J. A., MacArthur, C. A., Price, C., & Knight, D. (2011). Effects of a Structured Decoding Curriculum on Adult Literacy Learners' Reading Development. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555294

article_title: Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents
citation: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/
title: MSCEIT-YV Emotion Regulation Ability subtest
description: The ERA subtest from the Mayer, Salovey, and Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test—Youth Version measures "one's capacity to evaluate how effective different actions would be toward achieving a specific regulation goal". It presents six emotion-filled hypothetical scenarios describing everyday experiences relevant to adolescents, each followed by three potential actions the respondent rates for effectiveness toward a stated goal. Scoring uses expert scoring against judgments of emotion researchers, and scores are standardized to a mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15.
requirements: Respondents must read and evaluate hypothetical scenarios relevant to their developmental level
Scoring requires expert judgments guided by empirical research on effective emotion regulation strategies
constraints: Measures evaluation of strategies in hypothetical scenarios rather than enacted behavior in daily life
target_learning_goals: evaluating effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies
examples: One scenario describes Li, excited about an upcoming party but needing to study for an exam the next day, with respondents judging actions toward making Li study

Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/

citation: Wodtke, Geoffrey T.; Harding, David J.; Elwert, Felix. (2011). Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective. American Sociological Review. https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122411420816
title: Marginal structural models with inverse probability of treatment weighting for time-varying neighborhood exposures
description: The article adapts a counterfactual framework for time-varying treatments in which "Inverse probability of treatment (IPT) weighting is an alternative approach specifically developed to adjust for confounding by time-varying covariates." A marginal structural model specifies the logit of graduation as a function of duration-weighted exposure (the average of wave-specific quintile treatments). Weighting builds a pseudo-population in which treatment is unconfounded by measured covariates, allowing an unadjusted outcome model to yield unbiased causal effect estimates.
requirements: Assumptions of no unmeasured confounders, no model misspecification, and positivity (nonzero probability of exposure for every confounder combination)
Baseline covariates must still be conditioned on in the outcome model when using stabilized weights
constraints: Selection bias may remain if unobserved factors affect both residential choices and graduation; the no-unobserved-confounding assumption is not testable with the observed data
target_learners: children followed longitudinally in panel studies of residential context
target_learning_goals: causal estimation of cumulative environmental exposure effects on educational attainment
key_sources: Wodtke, Geoffrey T.; Harding, David J.; Elwert, Felix. (2011). Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective. American Sociological Review. https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122411420816

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study
citation: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5
title: Multi-strategy test (MST) vignette instrument for intended strategy application
description: The MST is a scenario-based test presenting "a fictitious learning situation in which students are asked to describe their intended approach to process the given learning task" in an open-response format. Two versions (MST_E for an experimentation task, MST_T for a text-highlighting task) are coded with a category system awarding up to 9 points for metacognitive skills and 9 for cognitive strategy steps. Double-coding a subsample of N = 60 (about 25% of the sample) yielded good inter-rater reliability with an average Cohen's of .91.
requirements: Requires spontaneous recall of skills and strategy steps without prompts; only conscious strategy knowledge can be named and recorded.
constraints: The MST measures intended application in a fictitious situation, not actual strategy application; the extent to which intended application reflects real application remains open, and scores may be influenced by the amount of text students produced.
target_learning_goals: assessment of spontaneous application of metacognitive skills and cognitive strategies
examples: MST_E asked students how they would find out what plants need to grow using an experiment; MST_T asked how they would proceed to summarize a multi-page magazine article for classmates.
key_sources: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5

article_title: Prospective Educational Applications of Mental Simulation: A Meta-review
citation: Meer, J.P. van & Theunissen, N.C.M. (2009). Prospective educational applications of mental simulation: A meta-review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9097-8
title: Five explanation models for why mental simulation works
description: The review presents five theoretical accounts of MS effectiveness: motivational, symbolic learning, attentional-arousal, bio-informational and psychoneuromuscular theory. The bio-informational theory "holds that every overt and covert behavior creates a specific and unique pattern of interconnected nodes in the brain", strengthened by rehearsal; symbolic learning ties MS effects to a task's cognitive component; psychoneuromuscular theory points to minute muscle innervations with EMG evidence. The authors note no clear-cut answer exists and models may jointly explain the phenomenon.
requirements: Future studies exploring how the models together explain MS effectiveness, as the authors recommend
constraints: The review states there is no clear-cut answer to why MS is effective; some researchers do not find the neuromuscular theory very likely
target_learners: healthy adults practicing motor or cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms of mental practice for skill performance enhancement
examples: EMG action potentials during MS are cited as physiological evidence; symbolic learning theory is used to explain why MS appears more useful for cognitive than physical tasks.
key_sources: Meer, J.P. van & Theunissen, N.C.M. (2009). Prospective educational applications of mental simulation: A meta-review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9097-8

article_title: Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education
citation: Chun-Yi Shen & Hsiu-Chuan Liu. (2011). Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Metacognitive Skills Evaluation Questionnaire (MSEQ)
description: The MSEQ is a 6-point Likert questionnaire with 45 items divided into four dimensions — self-plan (12 items), self-monitor (14 items), self-modify (9 items), and self-evaluate (10 items) — developed from the Metacognition Rating Scale for General Biology. It was tested through expert validity and construct validity tests before formal use, and "The overall Cronbach’s alpha of MSEQ was .92", with dimension alphas of .80, .82, .83, and .84. It served as both pretest and posttest, administered online.
requirements: The scale was tested through expert validity test and construct validity test before it was used in the formal test
target_learning_goals: measuring self-plan, self-monitor, self-modify, and self-evaluate skills
examples: Sample self-plan item: When I am learning, I usually set the goals first, and then decide what should be learned, and learn to what extent
key_sources: Chun-Yi Shen & Hsiu-Chuan Liu. (2011). Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ932234

article_title: Implementation of Research-Based ESL Strategies with Lower Grade Middle School ELLs in the Science Classroom: Findings from an Experimental Study
citation: Irby, B. J., Lara-Alecio, R., Tong, F., Guerrero, C., Sutton-Jones, K. L., & Abdelrahman, N. (2018). Implementation of Research-based ESL Strategies with Lower Grade Middle School ELLs in the Science Classroom: Findings from an Experimental Study. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language, 22(1). https://tesl-ej.org/
title: MSSELL literacy-infused science curriculum and bi-weekly professional learning for sixth-grade treatment teachers
description: Project MSSELL (DRL-0822343) provided treatment teachers ongoing bi-weekly, 90-minute, face-to-face professional learning sessions for one year, covering upcoming lessons and ESL strategies in researcher-developed, scripted lessons. Students received "85 minutes of daily literacy-infused science instruction" following a highly-structured curriculum aligned to state and national science and reading standards, embedding expository text features, pre-taught academic vocabulary, pronunciation and decoding, hands-on 5E activities, questioning, scaffolding, cooperative grouping, and technology integration.
requirements: Ongoing bi-weekly professional learning sessions taught by research coordinators specializing in science and second language development
constraints: The treatment curriculum replaced the district curriculum; randomization was at the school level and quasi-experimental at the student level in accordance with Texas law
target_learners: Sixth-grade English language learners and economically-challenged students in a large urban district in southeast Texas
target_learning_goals: Science content knowledge, academic English language, and literacy development
examples: Daily lessons used at least three of the 5E's, science notebooks, foldables, genre-based science writing, and EduSmart software segments with supplementary leveled questions
key_sources: Irby, B. J., Lara-Alecio, R., Tong, F., Guerrero, C., Sutton-Jones, K. L., & Abdelrahman, N. (2018). Implementation of Research-based ESL Strategies with Lower Grade Middle School ELLs in the Science Classroom: Findings from an Experimental Study. article_title: A Tool that Can be Effective in the Self-Regulated Learning of Pre-Service Teachers: The Mind Map
citation: Tanriseven, I. (2014). A Tool That Can Be Effective in the Self-regulated Learning of Pre-service Teachers: The Mind Map. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 39(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.14221/ajte.2014v39n1.1
title: Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ)
description: The MSLQ is "a self-report instrument designed to assess college students' motivational orientations and their use of different learning strategies for a college course", with a 31-item motivation section and 31 strategy items plus 19 resource-management items, rated on a seven-point Likert scale. Its fifteen modular scales can be used together or singly. The study used nine Turkish-adapted subscales with printed Cronbach alphas ranging from .41 (effort management) to .86 (self-efficacy).
requirements: Adapted and validated version for the target language population (Turkish adaptation by Büyüköztürk et al., 2004)
constraints: Effort management subscale reliability was low (Cronbach alpha = .41) in this administration
examples: Administered before and after the thirteen-week experiment to both groups.

article_title: The Effect of Collaborative Learning and Self-Assessment on Self-Regulation
citation: Ali Hatami. (2015). The effect of collaborative learning and self-assessment on self-regulation. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2349
title: MSLQ-based self-regulation measure and self-developed ten-question geometry achievement test
description: The study used "a part of the Pintrich and de Groot's motivated strategies for learning questionnaire (MSLQ)" together with a self-developed achievement test. The MSLQ version contained 22 questions on a five-point Likert scale measuring self-efficacy beliefs, beliefs about goals, and beliefs about values and interests. The achievement test consisted of ten questions, five measuring low levels of the cognitive domain and five the upper levels. Cronbach's alpha was used to assess validity of the results.
requirements: Administered as pre-test and post-test in all three groups
Reliability checked with Cronbach's alpha
constraints: The achievement test was self-developed by the author for geometry content
target_learning_goals: measuring self-regulated learning strategies and motivation
measuring geometry achievement across cognitive levels
examples: The MSLQ was administered at three levels and the achievement pre-test at two levels for all groups before the intervention

article_title: Is Case-Based Instruction Effective in Enhancing High School Students' Motivation toward Chemistry?
citation: Yalçınkaya, E., Boz, Y., & Erdur-Baker, Ö. (2012). Is case-based instruction effective in enhancing high school students' motivation toward chemistry? Science Education International, 23(2), 102-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ970613
title: Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) motivation section, Turkish adaptation
description: A self-report questionnaire measuring motivational orientations on a 7-point Likert scale, whose motivation section contains 31 items across six subscales: intrinsic goal orientation, extrinsic goal orientation, task value, control of learning beliefs, self-efficacy for learning and performance, and test anxiety. In this study "only the motivation section of MSLQ was used to determine the change of students' perceived motivation", using Sungur's (2004) Turkish adaptation piloted with 324 students, with Cronbach alphas reported per subscale.
requirements: Administered as pre- and post-test around the instruction period
constraints: The article states that both the English and Turkish versions of the MSLQ do not show good fit for the motivation section; GFI and AGFI values in the current study's CFA were below 0.9
target_learning_goals: Measuring perceived motivation (goal orientations, task value, control beliefs, self-efficacy, test anxiety)
examples: Used as pre- and post-test with the 45 participants; current-version Cronbach alphas ranged from 0.64 (task value) to 0.77 (test anxiety) as printed in Table 1

article_title: Effects of Making Sense of SCIENCE[TM] Professional Development on the Achievement of Middle School Students, Including English Language Learners. Final Report. NCEE 2012-4002
citation: Heller, J.I. (2012). Effects of Making Sense of SCIENCE™ professional development on the achievement of middle school students, including English language learners. (NCEE 2012-4002). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Making Sense of SCIENCE professional development theory of action: cascade from PD features to teacher knowledge to instruction to student achievement
description: The article describes a professional development logic model in which influences cascade "from features of the professional development to immediate impact on teacher knowledge, intermediate impacts on classroom instruction, and more distal effects on student achievement." The Making Sense of SCIENCE approach embodies this model by combining science content learning with analysis of student thinking and instructional strategies, plus language and literacy activities. The study tested the distal link of this cascade and found teacher knowledge gains but no significant student gains.
requirements: Teachers must have opportunities to learn science content knowledge in combination with analysis of student thinking about that content and instructional strategies for helping students learn it
constraints: The study did not measure classroom instruction, so the intermediate link of the cascade was untested
target_learners: grade 8 students including English language learners
target_learning_goals: science content knowledge of force and motion
examples: The trial tested the five-session course on force and motion with 181 teachers randomized across six regional sites
key_sources: Heller, J.I. (2012). Effects of Making Sense of SCIENCE™ professional development on the achievement of middle school students, including English language learners. (NCEE 2012-4002). title: Five key professional development features: content focus, active learning, coherence, duration, collective participation
description: The article enumerates the course's key features associated with increasing student achievement: "(a) in-depth focus on science content; (b) opportunities for teachers to engage in active learning; (c) coherence and alignment between the teacher curriculum and standards-based student curricula; (d) substantial duration and length of contact time, 24 hours over five days; and (e) a process of collective participation during which teachers engage in professional discourse and critical reflection." The course is built around hands-on science investigations and discussions of narrative teaching cases drawn from actual classroom episodes.
requirements: Contact time of 20 hours or more, per the duration evidence the article cites
constraints: The evidence regarding the necessity of extended school-year activities is not conclusive, per the article
examples: The five-day, 24-hour summer 2009 course on force and motion implemented these features at each of six sites with local facilitators

citation: Heller, J.I. (2012). Effects of Making Sense of SCIENCE™ professional development on the achievement of middle school students, including English language learners. (NCEE 2012-4002). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Course features implementing the CREDE Five Standards for Effective Pedagogy for students challenged by language or cultural barriers
description: Table 1.1 maps Making Sense of SCIENCE course features onto the CREDE Five Standards for Effective Pedagogy. Features include "Collaborative group science investigations and sense-making discussions," reading, writing, and speaking activities to develop academic language proficiency, hands-on activities based on natural phenomena, instructional tasks focused on making meaning of complex science ideas, and small-group opportunities for developing English proficiency through authentic communication about science ideas. A full quarter of the program focuses on identifying and evaluating literacy supports.
requirements: Teachers need strong and integrated knowledge of the science and knowledge of English language and literacy development to support English language learners
examples: Teachers planned discussion sequences with clear participation structures to help English language learners learn the rules of the game

article_title: Multimedia Scenario Based Learning Programme for Enhancing the English Language Efficiency among Primary School Students
citation: Tupe, N. (2015). Multimedia Scenario Based Learning Programme for Enhancing the English Language Efficiency among Primary School Students. International Journal of Instruction, 8(2). https://www.e-iji.net
title: Multimedia Scenario Based Learning Programme (MSBLP) for primary English
description: MSBLP is a remedial multimedia programme in which learning scenarios are built from Gagne's nine events of instruction and scenario-based learning approaches, delivered with animation, graphics, music and sound. It teaches twenty-three concepts (e.g. Profession, Direction, Food) drawn from grade 1-3 Maharashtra textbooks, each with its own small scenario, a fairy anchor who states objectives in Marathi, guided activities, feedback, and teacher facilitation and scaffolding. It was trialled as a three-month remedial programme for grade-3 students weak on grade-2 competencies.
requirements: Multimedia delivery with animation, graphics, audio and musical effects in flash player
A trained mentor or teacher to facilitate, scaffold and assess activities
constraints: Developed for Marathi-medium primary school students in Maharashtra
The article notes conversion of learning materials into ICT format is a major challenge for academicians and educators
target_learners: Grade-3 primary school students in Marathi-medium schools
target_learning_goals: Listening, speaking, understanding, reading and writing skills of English
examples: The programme was tried out in a sample school over three months, with one-hour English sessions on consecutive days each week, by teachers and PG students trained by the researcher.
key_sources: Tupe, N. (2015). Multimedia Scenario Based Learning Programme for Enhancing the English Language Efficiency among Primary School Students. International Journal of Instruction, 8(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085304

article_title: Medication safety in emergency departments: a mixed methods study.
citation: Tüzün Hande, Cebeci Fatma, Çetin Songül Bişkin. (2026). Medication safety in emergency departments: a mixed methods study. BMC Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12873-026-01615-7
title: Medication Safety Competence Scale for Nurses (MSCS), Turkish-validated version
description: The MSCS is a 36-item self-report instrument assessing medication safety competence across six subdimensions: patient-centered medication management, improvement of safety issues, management of influencing factors, safe risk management, multidisciplinary collaboration, and nursing responsibility. Items are rated on a five-point Likert scale, with higher scores indicating superior competence. The scale demonstrated excellent reliability in this study ("Cronbach's α = 0.953").
requirements: Respondents must be nurses directly involved in medication administration
constraints: Captures perceived competence and may not fully reflect enacted competence in real-time clinical practice
examples: Used in a census sample of 122 emergency nurses across two tertiary hospitals in Türkiye
key_sources: Tüzün Hande, Cebeci Fatma, Çetin Songül Bişkin. (2026). Medication safety in emergency departments: a mixed methods study. BMC Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12873-026-01615-7

article_title: Factors Associated With Medication Safety Competence Among Clinical Nurses in China: A Latent Profile Analysis.
citation: Zhang, P., Yu, G., Xu, R., Cao, S., Lin, M., Liu, Y., & Wu, Y. (2026). Factors associated with medication safety competence among clinical nurses in China: A latent profile analysis. The Journal of Nursing Research. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000749
title: Medication Safety Competence Scale (MSCS), Chinese version
description: A 36-item five-point Likert scale measuring medication safety competence across six factors, developed by Seomun and Park and translated into Chinese by Yang. Scores range from 36 to 180, with 36–90, 91–150, and 151–180 indicating poor, fair, and good competence respectively. The article reports "The Cronbach's α coefficient for the Chinese version of the MSCS was previously calculated as .940" and was .994 in this study.
requirements: Respondents must be registered nurses completing the self-report scale
constraints: Self-reported measure subject to recall and social-expectation biases, per the article's limitations
examples: Used as the primary outcome measure in the latent profile analysis of 1,228 Chinese nurses
key_sources: Zhang, P., Yu, G., Xu, R., Cao, S., Lin, M., Liu, Y., & Wu, Y. (2026). Factors associated with medication safety competence among clinical nurses in China: A latent profile analysis. The Journal of Nursing Research. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000749

article_title: Exploring the Interplay of Motivation, Self-Efficacy, Critical Thinking, and Self-Regulation in Predicting Academic Achievement Among University Students.
citation: Stavropoulou G, Daniilidou A, Nerantzaki K. (2025). Exploring the Interplay of Motivation, Self-Efficacy, Critical Thinking, and Self-Regulation in Predicting Academic Achievement Among University Students. F1000Research 14:344. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.161821.1
title: Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) subscales for motivation, self-efficacy, critical thinking, and self-regulation
description: The MSLQ by Pintrich (1991) is a self-report instrument assessing college students' motivational orientations and learning strategies. The article states "The questionnaire consists of 33 items, and participants respond on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (absolutely disagree) to 7 (absolutely agree)." In this study it provided subscales for intrinsic goal orientation (4 items), extrinsic goal orientation (4 items), self-efficacy (8 items, α = .92), critical thinking (5 items, α = .86), and self-regulation (12 items, α = .86), using a Greek translation.
requirements: A translated and validated version of the instrument for the target language and population, as the article used the Greek translation by Andreou and Metallidou (2004)
constraints: One extrinsic motivation item was removed in this sample because its factor loading was <.42, and extrinsic motivation reliability was α = .64
examples: The article administered the MSLQ via Google Forms and in-person distribution to 250 undergraduates, with achievement measured by self-reported mean grade

article_title: Teaching Medical Students to Help Patients Manage Their Weight: Outcomes of an Eight-School Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Ockene JK, Pbert L, Crawford S, Frisard CF, Pendharkar JA, Sadasivam RS, Faro J, Okuliar C, Eno C, Margo K, Shaw MA, Soleymani T, Stadler DD, Warrier S, White K, Geller AC. (2021). Teaching Medical Students to Help Patients Manage Their Weight: Outcomes of an Eight-School Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of General Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-020-06571-x
title: MSWeight multi-modal weight management counseling curriculum for medical students
description: MSWeight is a multi-modal education (MME) intervention implemented across medical school years 1–3, comprising "a 4-hour self-paced web course that is evidence-supported, competency-based and covers all 5As", a role-play exercise, a web-patient encounter with feedback, and an enhanced clerkship with preceptors trained in weight management counseling. Counseling focused on the 5As (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange) and patient-centeredness. Each component included written instructions, objectives, and discussion points to standardize delivery across schools. The curriculum was evaluated in an eight-school group-randomized trial against traditional education.
requirements: Preceptors attend a 30–60-minute session reviewing WMC guidelines and how to model, observe, instruct, and provide critical feedback on the 5As
Standardized written instructions, objectives, and discussion points for each component
constraints: Variability in medical schools requiring participation in the WMC curriculum; one school made participation voluntary
target_learning_goals: weight management counseling skills using the 5As approach
confidence in delivering health behavior change counseling
examples: In the trial, more than 2/3 of MME students completed all three intervention-delivered activities (67.9% completed all three components)
key_sources: Ockene JK, Pbert L, Crawford S, Frisard CF, Pendharkar JA, Sadasivam RS, Faro J, Okuliar C, Eno C, Margo K, Shaw MA, Soleymani T, Stadler DD, Warrier S, White K, Geller AC. (2021).
